Chromaticism uses notes outside the prevailing scale, often bringing semitone movement into melodies and chords.
Atonality is music without an established home key or the usual pull of dominant chords towards a tonic.
A twelve-note row places the twelve notes of the chromatic scale in an order that supplies a piece’s melodies and chords.
Modes are ways of arranging a scale around a home note, each with its own pattern of tones and semitones.
A whole-tone scale has six notes, with a whole tone between every neighbouring pair.
An octatonic scale has eight notes, with tones and semitones alternating.
Bitonality places two keys side by side in the same passage.
A suspension holds a note from one chord into the next, where it clashes before resolving down by step.
An appoggiatura is a leaning note that delays a chord note, usually on a strong beat, then resolves by step.
Modal mixture borrows notes or chords from the major or minor scale that shares a piece’s tonic.
A lament bass descends from the tonic to the dominant, often repeating beneath a song of grief.
Counterpoint combines melodic lines that keep their own shape and rhythm while sounding together.
Imitation occurs when one voice repeats a melody or fragment just heard in another voice.
A canon is a melody followed by another voice that keeps imitating it at a fixed distance in time.
Homophony gives one melody the lead while the other parts supply its harmony.
An ostinato is a short musical pattern repeated persistently while the music around it changes.
